newsitem.title: USA: Crop scouts to benefit from more mature corn, soy.
newsitem.headline: Crop scouts to benefit from more mature corn, soy.

text.p: The advanced maturity of the U.S. Midwest corn crop compared with the past couple of years will enable a more accurate yield estimate from crop scouts on this year's Pro Farmer-sponsored Midwest Crop Tour.

"The number one thing I am most excited about is the corn crop maturity is further along than in '95 and '96," said Pro Farmer's Chip Flory, the director of the annual tour. "The more mature the crop, the higher is the likelihood we'll get a more accurate read on yield."

The Midwest corn crop as of Sunday, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture, was 96 percent pollinated which was well ahead of a year ago when corn was 86 percent pollinated and above average of 88 percent.
Pollination or "silking", is the reproductive phase of corn development and weather events during the pollination phase figures largely in final crop yields.
Twenty-eight percent of the crop was in the dough stage of development as of Sunday, ahead of 21 percent a year ago and about even with the 29 percent average.

The pollination process for the U.S. crop should be virtually complete by Monday, the start date for this year's crop tour which covers Ohio, Illinois, Indiana, Minnesota, Iowa, Nebraska, South Dakota and Missouri.
The tour is slated to begin early Tuesday in Dayton, Ohio and end late Friday in Des Moines, Iowa.
USDA this week surprised the market by forecasting the 1997 U.S. corn crop at 9.276 billion bushels, well below an average of analysts' estimates for 9.554 billion bushels.
But the government crop number was based on conditions existing in the U.S. as of August 1. The corn crop has undergone a rapid maturing process since then.
"When the crop is immature there is so much potential involved it's hard to get an accurate yield estimate," Flory said.
The 1996 U.S. corn crop totalled 9.293 billion bushels, according to the USDA, which was well above a wide range of expectations that circulated during last summer's growing season.
The Illinois corn per acre yield last year was 136 bushels, USDA said. The Pro Farmer tour last August pegged the Illinois corn yield per acre at 133.2 bushels per acre.
But Iowa was the "wild card" in 1996 and the government pegged that state's actual yield per acre at 138 bushels, well above the tour estimate of 126.5 bushels per acre.
Flory, in a letter to crop scouts, conceded the difficulty during 1996 in forecasting corn yields.

"What 1996 taught me was this: Don't underestimate the potential of the crop if the plant population is acceptable, weather is simply too unpredictable and anticipating even normal conditions can be the wrong choice," Flory wrote.

The U.S. soybean crop will undergo scrutiny as tour participants count pods in each field which again only indicates potential production. The tour group will be estimating the number of soybean pods per acre, Flory said.
USDA Tuesday estimated the 1997 U.S. soybean crop at a record 2.744 billion bushels.
"Another thing is the maturity of the crop and just how widespread the moisture shortage is and we can do this (determine soil moisture levels) on soybeans," he said.

Dry weather in July and early August caused concern about cuts in crop production prospects in some Midwest areas, especially central and southern Illinois. But rains this week should stem declines in production potential for those areas.
